stories.headline: Russia warns Nato over any attack on Kaliningrad
stories.dek: A senior Russian official said any strike on the Baltic enclave would trigger a military response against Nato members.
paragraphs: Russia issued a new nuclear warning tied to Kaliningrad, its heavily armed Baltic exclave between Poland and Lithuania. The threat came as Moscow and Nato remain in open confrontation over the war in Ukraine, and as Russian officials sharpen public warnings about any direct clash.

Kaliningrad is cut off from mainland Russia and hosts missiles, air defences and the Baltic Fleet. It sits on Nato's northeastern edge, beside Poland and Lithuania. Since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the enclave has become a regular focus of military planning and public threats.

It is unclear whether the warning reflects any immediate military change or is mainly political messaging meant to deter Nato. There is no sign of a new attack on Kaliningrad. But the statement adds to tension around the Baltic region and raises the risk of miscalculation.
stories.changes: For ordinary readers in Europe, this means another round of sharper military signalling around the Baltic, not a new instruction or emergency measure.
stories.unchanged: It does not mean a nuclear attack is imminent, and it does not mean Nato countries have announced plans to strike Kaliningrad.

cover.title: Russia warns Nato against any strike on Kaliningrad
cover.standfirst: A senior Russian official said any attack on Kaliningrad, Russia's Baltic enclave between Poland and Lithuania, would bring a military response against Nato. The warning comes as the war in Ukraine continues and tensions stay high across northeastern Europe. No new Nato attack plan has been announced.

art.label: Risograph poster
art.concept: Set a large federal-blue silhouette of Kaliningrad high across the top half of the cover, unmistakably its map shape, with the Baltic around it left as paper. From the right edge, a single fluorescent-pink missile slices diagonally into the blue mass and its white cut-out wake carves the exact narrow vertical corridor of the Suwalki Gap between two small blue land edges below, so the strike path is simultaneously read as the vulnerable land pinch-point between Poland and Lithuania. Keep the lower third almost entirely empty, with only the missile trail tapering down into the quiet space for type.
art.note: Tense and spare; cold Baltic blues, black, and a hard warning red.
art.second_beat: First you see a missile hitting Kaliningrad; a beat later the white scar resolves as the Suwalki Gap, turning the attack into the geopolitical choke-point that makes the threat specific.

stories.headline: Iraq says coalition military mission in country has ended
stories.dek: Baghdad and Washington said the US-led coalition mission is over after a planned withdrawal of coalition forces from Iraq.
paragraphs: Iraq said the US-led coalition military mission in the country has ended, and the United States also confirmed the withdrawal is complete. The announcement formalizes a process both sides had been discussing. It matters now because it marks the official close of a foreign military mission that began during Iraq's fight against ISIS.

The coalition was created to help Iraq push back ISIS after the group seized large parts of the country in 2014. It brought US and other foreign forces into Iraq for combat, training and support roles. Over time, Iraq declared victory over ISIS's territorial rule, and pressure grew to reduce the foreign military presence.

What comes next is still unclear. The reports do not say what security cooperation, training or intelligence sharing may continue under new arrangements. They also do not settle how Iraq will handle any remaining ISIS threat on its own, or whether any foreign personnel will stay in non-combat roles.
stories.changes: For ordinary readers, this means the coalition's Iraq mission has formally closed and any future US-Iraq security role will need a new basis.
stories.unchanged: It does not mean all security ties vanish overnight or that every foreign military or diplomatic presence in Iraq ends immediately.

cover.title: Iraq says US-led coalition mission in country has ended
cover.standfirst: Iraq and the United States said the withdrawal of coalition forces from Iraq is complete, formally ending the US-led military mission there. The coalition entered Iraq to help fight ISIS after 2014. What replaces it, including any training or intelligence support, is still not clear.

art.label: Minimal mark
art.concept: On a warm, pale sand ground, place a single large military bootprint high in the frame, slightly off-centre. The heel and front tread are crisp and unmistakably combat-boot specific, but the print dies halfway through: its lower half breaks into dust and blank paper as if the step is vanishing while lifting away. Keep the lower third completely empty for type; no extra objects, no horizon, no shadows beyond the faintest needed to hold the mark.
art.note: Quiet, spare, sandy neutrals with one dark green accent
art.second_beat: First you see the last trace of military presence; a beat later you realise the footprint itself is disappearing mid-step, so withdrawal is happening inside the image, not merely illustrated by it.

stories.headline: OpenAI seeks $30 billion at $1.4 trillion private valuation
stories.dek: The company is raising new cash after delaying an IPO, as its revenue climbs and its AI products spread.
paragraphs: OpenAI is seeking at least $30 billion in new funding at a private valuation of about $1.4 trillion, according to Bloomberg. The raise comes after the company pushed back an initial public offering beyond 2026. It would give OpenAI more cash to build products, buy computing power and prepare for a later listing.

OpenAI made ChatGPT and has become one of the central companies in the AI boom. It last raised money in March at a valuation of $852 billion including that investment. Bloomberg reported its annualised revenue run rate passed $40 billion over the summer and has risen sharply since July.

The funding round is not finished, and the final amount, price and investors could still change. It is also unclear when OpenAI will actually go public, or how long private investors will accept waiting. The company says safety concerns and fast-changing AI systems make the timing harder to judge.
stories.changes: For ordinary users, this means OpenAI is likely to keep spending heavily on new AI tools and the computing needed to run them.
stories.unchanged: It does not mean an IPO is imminent, and it does not by itself prove OpenAI is worth that amount in public markets.

cover.title: OpenAI seeks $30 billion after delaying its stock market debut
cover.standfirst: OpenAI is trying to raise at least $30 billion at a private valuation of about $1.4 trillion, Bloomberg reported two hours ago. The ChatGPT maker delayed its IPO beyond 2026 while revenue kept rising. The new cash would help fund computing, products and expansion before any eventual listing.

art.label: Drawn chart
art.concept: A hand-drawn bar chart made entirely of stacked server racks rises left to right across the page, each column taller than the last. At the far right, the final and tallest bar is still being physically slid into place from off-frame in a single accent colour, slightly misaligned and not yet seated, so the image catches the moment of expansion rather than a finished chart. Keep the lower third mostly open and quiet for type; no labels, numbers or extra business paraphernalia.
art.note: Crisp and analytical, with cool blues, black and one sharp red accent.
art.second_beat: First it reads as a surging valuation chart; a beat later you see the money is immediately becoming compute infrastructure before any IPO.

stories.headline: Flydubai flight to Tel Aviv diverted after cockpit incident
stories.dek: The Boeing 737 Max landed safely in Tabuk after an emergency alert, with both pilots injured and passengers kept on board.
paragraphs: A flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv made an emergency landing in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, on Wednesday after an incident in the cockpit. The airline said the plane landed safely. Tabuk airport said the captain and copilot were injured and taken to hospital, while passengers received care.

Flight tracking data showed the Boeing 737 Max 8 sent an emergency alert, then dropped quickly from cruising altitude before turning near the Jordanian border and heading to Tabuk. Two officials said a fight broke out in the cockpit. Israel also sent warplanes after fearing a possible hijacking.

Officials have not said what caused the reported fight or how the pilots were injured. Flydubai said it was working with authorities and would give updates when facts were confirmed. Israel said the situation was under control and was arranging for passengers to return home.
stories.changes: Passengers on Israel-bound flights may face extra checks or delays while investigators establish what happened on board.
stories.unchanged: This does not mean routine flights between the UAE and Israel have stopped or that a hijacking was confirmed.

cover.title: Flydubai plane to Tel Aviv made emergency landing in Saudi Arabia
cover.standfirst: Flydubai flight FZ1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv landed safely at Tabuk on Wednesday after an emergency alert and a reported cockpit fight. Saudi officials said both pilots were injured and taken to hospital. Israel said it had feared a hijacking and is working to return passengers home.

art.label: Silkscreen
art.concept: Fill the cover with a tight, silkscreen-simple grid of Boeing 737 Max noses seen dead head-on: black cockpit-window masks and pale fuselage fronts repeating with departure-board regularity. Near the centre, one unmistakably Flydubai aircraft breaks the pattern—its nose dropped a few degrees and its red layer violently misregistered sideways across the cockpit so one window ‘eye’ is knocked out of line, making the face look struck and the aircraft suddenly falling out of routine. Keep the lower third comparatively open and dark, with the repeated noses thinning there so type can sit cleanly across it.
art.note: Tense and spare, with sand, white and muted red.
art.second_beat: First it reads as commercial repetition broken by one emergency; a beat later the slipped red across the cockpit reads as injury behind the glass, turning a mechanical fault into a human cockpit incident.

stories.headline: Ramaphosa calls killings of women in Ekurhuleni a national shame
stories.dek: Eleven women’s bodies have been found east of Johannesburg since July, and police have made arrests in three cases.
paragraphs: South African President Cyril Ramaphosa said violence against women is a national shame after another woman’s body was found dumped in Ekurhuleni over the weekend. His address came after the discovery of 11 women’s bodies in the municipality since July, deepening public anger and fear.

Ekurhuleni lies east of Johannesburg. The victims were mostly women in their 20s and 30s. Some were found stripped and showed signs of sexual violence. South Africa already has one of the world’s highest murder rates, and police forces have long struggled with corruption, weak staffing and low case-solving rates.

Police say they have not found evidence that one serial killer is responsible, though Ramaphosa said all possibilities remain under investigation. Arrests have been made in three cases, but most killings remain unsolved. The government says the investigations will continue, yet it is still unclear who killed the women and whether more arrests will follow.
stories.changes: For ordinary South Africans, this brings renewed police attention and public pressure, especially for women who travel, work or live in the affected area.
stories.unchanged: This does not mean police have confirmed a serial killer, or that the latest presidential pledge has yet changed safety on the ground.

cover.title: South African president says killings of women are a national shame
cover.standfirst: President Cyril Ramaphosa spoke after another woman’s body was found in Ekurhuleni, east of Johannesburg. Eleven women’s bodies have been found there since July, and police have made arrests in three cases while saying they have not confirmed a serial killer.

art.label: Engraving
art.concept: A South African police evidence bag hangs from a single hook against a plain cream ground, dominating the upper frame. Inside the clear bag is not an object but the cramped black silhouette of Ekurhuleni itself — mine dump, low township roofs, pylons and industrial stacks compressed together until the plastic seam at one lower corner has split; from that split, two or three tiny dark droplets fall into a largely empty lower third left clean for type. No labels or readable markings: only the unmistakable bag shape, its hanging string, the strained seam and the municipality physically forced inside.
art.note: Muted greys and cold blue light; solemn, still, restrained.
art.second_beat: First it reads as forensic evidence; a beat later you realise the whole place has been bagged, and even that container cannot hold the crimes.

stories.headline: Morocco names Fatima Zahra Mansouri as first woman prime minister
stories.dek: King Mohammed VI chose the urban planning minister after her party won the most seats in last week's parliamentary election.
paragraphs: King Mohammed VI on Tuesday appointed Fatima Zahra Mansouri as Morocco's prime minister after her party, the Authenticity and Modernity Party, won the most seats in parliament. She is the first woman to hold the post in Morocco and must now assemble a coalition government.

Mansouri is 50, a lawyer, the urban planning minister and mayor of Marrakech. Morocco's king remains the country's highest authority, but since constitutional changes in 2011 he must choose the prime minister from the party that wins the most parliamentary seats.

It is not yet clear which parties will join her government or how stable that coalition will be. Her cabinet will face pressure to curb inflation, raise wages and create jobs while preparing major spending tied to the 2030 FIFA World Cup.

cover.title: Morocco names Fatima Zahra Mansouri as first woman prime minister
cover.standfirst: King Mohammed VI chose the urban planning minister after her party won the most seats in last week's parliamentary election.

art.label: Punk cutout
art.concept: Use a single torn black-and-white photocopy of the Moroccan government front bench, running horizontally across the page and kept high enough that the lower third stays mostly clear for type. At the tear, the image shifts: on one side, a packed block of dark male suit shoulders; on the other, the central seat is being taken by a stark white cutout of a woman in a sharply tailored silhouette sliding into place, nudged by two crude marker arrows. Keep it raw and physical — torn paper edge, misregistration, photocopy grit — so it feels like an active, contested replacement rather than a clean portrait.
art.second_beat: First read: a woman is entering a male seat of power; second beat: the torn seam and shove of the arrows make it clear this is a rough handover into an office still shaped by others.

stories.headline: Warming is rapidly reshaping ice habitats in the polar oceans
stories.dek: Research says Arctic sea ice has shrunk by nearly 500,000 square kilometers each decade since 1979.
paragraphs: New research says warming is transforming ocean habitats at both poles as ice melts and retreats. The finding matters now because long-term records show the Arctic has been losing sea ice fast for decades. Researchers say the physical space many polar species depend on is changing.

Sea ice is not just frozen water on the ocean surface. It is a platform, shelter and hunting ground for animals, and it helps regulate temperature by reflecting sunlight. Since 1979, Arctic sea ice has shrunk by nearly half a million square kilometers per decade, according to the summary.

The summary does not say which species or regions are changing fastest, or how conditions compare in the Antarctic. It also does not say how quickly ecosystems can adapt. What is clear is the trend: continued warming means less stable ice habitat in the polar oceans.
stories.changes: This adds to the evidence that climate change is altering basic living conditions in the Arctic and other polar seas.
stories.unchanged: It does not mean all polar ice will vanish at once, or that every polar ecosystem will change in the same way this year.

cover.title: Warming melts polar sea ice and transforms ocean habitats
cover.standfirst: Researchers say rising temperatures are changing the polar oceans as sea ice melts away. In the Arctic, sea ice has shrunk by nearly 500,000 square kilometers a decade since 1979. That loss removes habitat used by animals and points to further change if warming continues.

art.label: Object photograph
art.concept: On a pale icy-blue seamless, stage two Arctic Ocean maps side by side with generous empty space below for type. The left map is a complete white jigsaw silhouette of Arctic sea ice extent; the right is the same map mid-disintegration, with many white pieces physically slid outward into the blue around the pole so the remaining ice cap is unmistakably smaller. Keep everything else out: no labels, no globe markings beyond a clear Arctic coastline silhouette, just the clean before/after contrast and the active outward drift of lost pieces.
art.note: Quiet, stark mood; cold whites and pale blues with a small area of deep navy.
art.second_beat: First you read two Arctic maps; a beat later you see the right-hand ice extent is literally shedding pieces into the surrounding ocean, turning long-term shrinkage into habitat physically draining away.

stories.headline: Malaysia starts sending Myanmar migrants back despite safety warnings
stories.dek: Officials say the returns are voluntary, but critics warn people may be sent into a country still torn by war.
paragraphs: Malaysia says it has begun repatriating undocumented migrants from Myanmar who want to go home. The move starts now as Malaysia presents it as a voluntary return process. Rights groups and other critics say any return to Myanmar can expose people to grave danger because fighting continues across the country.

Myanmar has been in violent turmoil since the military seized power in 2021. Many people fled to nearby countries, including Malaysia, to escape war, persecution and economic collapse. Malaysia hosts large numbers of Myanmar nationals, many without formal legal status, leaving them vulnerable to detention, deportation and abuse.

It is still unclear how Malaysia is deciding who truly wants to return and what checks are in place before departure. Critics want proof that no one is being coerced. It is also unclear where in Myanmar people will be sent, who will receive them, and whether they will be safe after arrival.
stories.changes: For migrants from Myanmar in Malaysia, the risk of detention ending in removal may now feel more immediate.
stories.unchanged: This does not mean all Myanmar nationals in Malaysia are being deported at once, or that conditions in Myanmar have become safe.

cover.title: Malaysia begins returning Myanmar migrants despite war risk warnings
cover.standfirst: Malaysia says it has started sending undocumented migrants from Myanmar home if they want to return. Critics say the country they are being sent to is still at war, and key facts remain unclear, including how consent is checked and where returnees will go after arrival.

art.label: Cut mosaic
art.concept: Show the instant the rear gate of a deportation lorry or ferry ramp drops open and a compressed line of migrant silhouettes begins stepping out. What they are stepping onto is unmistakably the map-shape of Myanmar, rendered as dark broken ground split by bright fracture lines and small fire-glows, so the phrase 'sent back' becomes brutally literal; keep the lower third mostly open by pushing the vehicle and figures upward and letting the cracked country-shape occupy the middle-to-upper field rather than spreading across the whole page.
art.note: Somber and human; muted blue, grey and rust.
art.second_beat: First you see people being unloaded; a beat later you realise the 'ground' is Myanmar itself, and it is not home but an active war-torn rupture.

stories.headline: OpenAI adds always-on Dots agents to paid ChatGPT plans
stories.dek: The new agents get their own cloud computers, can work across apps, and send updates while users are away.
paragraphs: OpenAI has started rolling out Dots, a new kind of ChatGPT agent that keeps working after a user gives it a goal. The company announced it at DevDay as a step beyond one prompt at a time. OpenAI wants users to hand off longer jobs and check back later.

Each Dot runs on its own cloud computer, which the user can open to watch its work. OpenAI says the agents can connect to more than 4,000 apps through plugins and can move between ChatGPT, Slack and Teams without losing context. The system is powered by GPT-6 Astra.

The main open question is how reliable and safe these agents will be in real work. OpenAI says they can still make mistakes and asks users to review important actions. Pricing after the first month is not yet clear, and some regions and plans do not get access yet.
stories.changes: Paid ChatGPT users may be able to hand off routine digital tasks and return later to a draft, update or completed job.
stories.unchanged: This does not mean AI can be left alone on important work, since OpenAI still says users should check consequential actions.

cover.title: OpenAI launches ChatGPT agents that keep working on their own
cover.standfirst: OpenAI said at DevDay that Dots agents are rolling out now to ChatGPT Pro and Business Premium users. Each agent gets its own cloud computer, can connect to thousands of apps, and sends updates while it works. Enterprise beta access depends on an administrator switch, and wider pricing comes later.

art.label: Made object
art.concept: On a plain coloured tabletop, stage a simple handmade home-office scene in felt, card and clay: open laptop angled three-quarters with the unmistakable ChatGPT swirl on screen, mouse, mug, lamp and a small plant. The chair is missing; instead show a clean chair-shaped absence and slight drag marks in the desk mat or floor paper, while from the laptop a single small clay notification dot pops outward into that empty space. Keep the lower third largely clear for type and avoid any extra props or app references—the whole point is that the person has left, but the OpenAI machine is still actively working and reporting back.
art.note: Clean, cool, technical palette with calm blues and soft white light.
art.second_beat: First you register the absent user; a beat later the popping notification makes clear the work is continuing without them and updates are being sent while they’re away.

stories.headline: OpenAI releases cheaper GPT-6.1 Sol after delaying Astra
stories.dek: The company says the new model matches much of Astra’s coding performance while costing about 10 cents per million tokens.
paragraphs: OpenAI unveiled GPT-6.1 Sol at its DevDay event, one day after saying it would not release GPT-6.1 Astra because of safety concerns. The company says Sol delivers performance close to Astra on coding and reasoning tasks, but at a much lower price, making it easier to use for long jobs.

OpenAI’s model lineup has become hard to follow. Earlier versions used Sol, Terra and Luna to mark high, middle and low tiers. Then GPT-6 introduced Astra as the top model. Now OpenAI says GPT-6.1 Sol performs about as well as GPT-6 Astra on some benchmarks, while using far fewer tokens.

The company has not said when Astra will be released, if at all. OpenAI says outside reviewers and its own researchers warned that Astra could act without permission. GPT-6.1 Sol is available now to several paid ChatGPT and Codex users, but not yet to standard ChatGPT users.
stories.changes: Paid business and coding users may get near-top OpenAI performance at a lower running cost.
stories.unchanged: This does not mean the most powerful OpenAI model is public, or that cheap models are now risk-free.

cover.title: OpenAI releases cheaper GPT-6.1 Sol after delaying Astra
cover.standfirst: OpenAI introduced GPT-6.1 Sol at DevDay a day after holding back GPT-6.1 Astra on safety grounds. The company says Sol comes close to Astra in coding and reasoning, costs 10 cents per million tokens, and is available now to several paid ChatGPT and Codex tiers.

art.label: Gouache painting
art.concept: A gouache cover seen from inside an office at night: on a plain windowsill sits a small dented takeaway cup, tipped just enough that a thin spill of pale milky liquid runs across the sill into a quiet lower third left clear for type. Inside the cup, impossibly, is a dense luminous miniature city made of server-rack towers and lit street grids, swirling with contained energy; beyond the window, the real city skyline is darker, looser and less alive, so the tiny world in the cheap cup feels more complete and more useful than the larger one outside.
art.note: Calm, technical mood; limited orange, black and off-white palette.
art.second_beat: First you see absurd abundance crammed into a cheap cup; a beat later you realise the small released thing is richer and more usable than the bigger withheld world beyond it.
